blocks.x: You can start giving your name first.
Honest MacLean.
Is there any middle initials?
Honest Joseph MacLean.
And if you can tell just where you were born? 1925. And what was the exact birth date?
Middle 23, 1925.
And where were you born? Which part of town were you living down in this section was it? About that time?
I think your father said... It was just right across Claybone Street. On St. Philip here?
Yeah, in 1900's.
By Philip and Rome.

Can you remember the very first music you ever heard? When you were even a little kid, you know, barely able to walk? Maybe some people can't remember back that far, but... I mean, the first bands, do you remember any parades or bands or dance bands any time when you were a boy that you'd follow?
Well, I think I remember my godfather's band.
Who was that? Kid Rene. Oh, Kid Rene was your godfather. Yeah.
I think that was in the... Around the other 30's. I was real small then, I was seven years old. Yeah. I remember that.
How come you took up guitar? Just because there was always one around the house? Or were you crazy about music when you started there all the time?
Because the instrument was around the house really, because I admired trumpet and saxophone.
And piano.
And I think I was 11 years old when my father first got a guitar.
Mm-hmm.
And I was still there.
Did you try to pick it up and learn it yourself? Did your father try to encourage you or did he help you with it right away? Or did he... Didn't want you to fool with his instrument?
He taught me cars. And I started from just learning strum cars.
Did you learn to read right away or did...
Not right away.
More by year.
I guess I was playing about two or three years before I learned to read.
About how old were you then?
I was 11 years old.
About 11 at that time when you started to learn to read too. That's pretty early age.
No, I was...let me see. When I learned to read I was maybe 14 or 15 years old. A little older than that. Because I didn't pick up the guitar until I was 11 years old. Yeah. So... I think I was...

I played violin all my life which is a small instrument but that guitar still seemed so big to me. Can a kid that age handle a big guitar or did you get a smaller one or what did you do? It's awfully big neck for a little kid isn't it? Could you handle it alright?

To me they didn't make the guitars as large as the one I have right now. It was a smaller neck. A smaller guitar. Well I didn't have too much trouble with the neck guitar. When I really got started is when I went to the service. My father taught me before I went to the service.
Did you...with your father did you have regular lessons every week? Or a certain time? Or just whenever you could catch him to have time?
Just whenever he had time. Sometime it would be every day. Every day.
You had an advantage there then.

No. And...well...when he started waking at the daytime. I think he was working at the WPA band during that time I think. And...well he had to stop fooling around with me everyday like that. Yeah. So you had to wait maybe until Saturdays or Sundays you know when we get together. Yeah. And he had a couple other fellas coming during that time. And that made me take more of my interest in the instruments you know. That's when I began to learn how to read more. Yeah.
Did you ever play any music in the schools? Which school did you go to?
No I was in grammar school down here. At Crate.
Yeah. Did they have any band or orchestra of any kind in the music? I didn't get no band in school.
No.
Did they teach the kids to read music in the schools in those days? Sometimes they do other times they don't. And with their singing and all. Did they teach them to read ever in your school?
Well...the kids they had in the band in school when I was going to school I don't think they could play without reading. Yeah.

It's usually that way. I just wondered...I mean all of the children, everybody in the whole grade, did they all have to learn to read music? No. When I went to school they tried to teach everybody in the school. You know, in order to sing... Oh you mean just the average... Just the average kid in the school. Just the average kid in the school. Didn't take up any instruments. No. I wondered if they taught that here in the schools ever here.
Not too much of it, no.
Do you remember the first band you ever played with or group or first job you ever got when you decided you'd be good enough to go out and try to play?

The first band I really enjoyed playing with after I began to read pretty good. You know, Don Raymond. I worked with Kit Howard before that and I had kind of a hard time. I couldn't catch on to a lot of the things they were doing. No.

No. Do you know most of those pieces from hearing people around? That is, I don't know if you were too small to go to dances naturally when you were a kid, but like all these old Dixieland tunes as they call them, did you know most of those or the pieces they played just from hearing them? Like maybe sometime on the street the brass band plays them. Did you ever, or did you have to really work hard to learn all of those tunes? Like, well say even St. Louis Blues or Tiger Rag or different things they play quite often.
Well I remember playing St. Louis Blues, Tiger Rag, Bill Bok, Bell Poker, China Bar, some of the tunes I liked.
I know, Kit Howard knows so many pieces, he's unusual, he knows so many numbers.
And he played quite a few waltzes too.
You have to learn the waltzes too.
Well I got experience by doing that too. And just like I said, they called numbers that I never heard before and I had trouble with them.
And they tried to fake them.
And they tried to fake them. Well I think I took more interest in the instrument when I went to the service. I left Don Raymond's band going to service. That was World War II.
Yeah, but what year is it, 40?
Well it was not quite a year.
42 or so along in there?
Yeah, just about 10 months after the war began.
And uh...

You see, like... There's like today, your problem with a part about these powers, you see? Yes. When they're broadcasting and...
Oh, yes. It's better to find a fine sounding group.

With this band here? Oh, all of them.

Well, we might go out and talk a little bit more about your guitar now.
What is the color?

No, I didn't have electric guitars.
You use electric nowadays?
I do, yeah.
When did you start on, get that? What kind of an instrument is it? What make?
I have a Gibson guitar. In fact, I've been using Gibson practically all my life.

Supposed to be a good make, I guess you like it then. I was going to ask more about the lessons with your father. Did he teach you with adjusted chart or did you get a guitar book with him pretty soon or what?
Well, he taught me for, he taught a lot of books and sheet music at times and different other little instrumental solos. Yeah. You know, like that.
Well, the MacNeil method was the method I taught him. He was MacNeil method. MacNeil method.
That's right.
I brought him clean through the MacNeil method. Who publishes that?

Well, it's published by him.
I didn't know if it was somebody like Carl Fisher or somebody like that.
No, I have a Carl Fisher's book, alright, but it's nothing.

I'm going to ask you if you ever did any picking with your fingers, you know, like the classical guitar, the Spanish guitar players like Segovia and all, where they'll pick, you know, where they'll pick with all of their, about three fingers and their thumb, or if you just always used the pick to strum it, what style of guitar?

Well, I did, but I wasn't too successful with it. I think I waited a little too late for that. So you've always used the pick? I've always used the pick. The pick style. I would like to study it, but if I had, you know, time to put it into it. Maybe I could, you know, do a little stuff. Did you, uh, like the guitar.

I mentioned before, we started the tape that Johnny St. Cyr mentioned that he thought you had such a wonderful style on your solos and all, that if he ever had a band, he'd like to play the rhythm guitar himself and have you as a featured soloist on guitar.
Yeah, I recorded some records with him three or four years ago.
Oh, you did?
Uh-huh. My father was on records with us, too. Uh-huh.

John-
John- John- John-

Well, in that particular session I did. Nothing but a single string work, wasn't it? Yeah. Yeah.
Uh-huh. I was going to ask the kind of strings you use too. Some people use only nylon strings or, uh, do you use all metal strings?
No. Right now I'm using that, uh, chrome nickel.
Chrome nickel.
It's, uh, a foreign made of strings, a labella strings.
Uh-huh.

I think there's a, there's quite a few, uh, factories, manufacturing that, uh, chrome nickel. I think. Gibson has them, and, uh, Gretsch and Epiliform. Yeah. Most all of them have it now, you know. I mean, I've been using labella, chrome nickel. Uh-huh. Uh-huh.
Do you play anywhere regularly around town?
Well, I'm doing spot, spot jobs, not with Dave Bartholomew.
Dave Bartholomew. Uh-huh.
We, uh, mostly recognized as a rock and roll band. We do a variety of things.
Yes, I understand. In order to make, uh, make a go of it today, you just about have to play rock and roll. Yeah.
We do a variety of things, but they say rock and roll. Uh-huh.

Rock and roll.

No.
You never did sing?

No.

Oh, really? I didn't even know. You see, they've...
Most everything he cut in town, I don't remember.
Yeah, most of those, they don't put the names of the band on, you know. Some records do, but his don't, I don't believe, usually.
And, uh, when I first started recording, I started recording with, uh, Rob Brown. Uh-huh. I was supposed to make the, uh, Round About Midnight, you know, Round About Midnight?
No.
The Rock of Midnight with him. Uh-huh. And something happened, I didn't get on that, that session. And right after that, Fats Domino came to the scene, and, uh, and caught it.
Just about when did Fats Domino make those first records that made the big hits? How long ago, can you remember?
Well, uh, the Fat Man was the one that's supposed to have gotten started.
You remember about what year? I think that was around, 51.
About 1951, that long. That long ago, I couldn't remember.

Uh, were there any other bands in there we could go back to your life after you played, uh, you say you played with Kid Howard there for a while? And then, uh, any other, the more or less Dixieland type bands, or dance bands you played with after that that you can remember?
Well, I worked around with, uh, around town with, uh, Manny Gabriel. Uh-huh. He's in, uh, yeah.
You played with Paul Barbera?
Yeah. Well, you played with Paul Barbera? Right after coming out of the service, I played with Paul Barbera. Yeah, I never heard you in those days, you see.

46th.
Then you were playing straight with Paul Barbera.
Right after I came out of the service.

Well, he admired my single spring work, I think, and solo work.
Uh-huh.
Yeah. I used to do a lot of that with him. But, you know, change and mental all the time. I think I worked with him at six months, you know? At six months. You know, that's...
I worked at the famous door with Edgar Blanchett, and two guitars, and...
Vibes and bass.
Remember the names of the other fellows that were in the group?
Well, we had Dawgert Dawson and Vibes. Stuart Davis, played bass with us. And Edgar was the other guitar player. Yeah. Edgar got his own band and... I was in my Natal, I think.
Have you traveled around the country very much?

Or... Well, uh... I'm 51. Right after... Right after... recording around town... No, I think it was right after... After I came from California. Because I was living in this house. I worked with Dave Martholomeo at... 48... 47 and 48, I think. Mm-hmm.
And I left...
I left him... And... To go with Joe Liggins. I left town with Joe Liggins. Oh, yeah. And I wound up in California. So... Yeah.
Were you out in California very long?
I stayed there about three months.
Well, you had a job that day or working that day with him? I was working with him.
Were you on that honey dripper? And I left California to come back on the road with him. Were you on that honey dripper record by any chance?
No.
That was his big hit, wasn't it?
That's the thing that made him popular.

Well, that was before... Before your time. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. And I came back to town and worked with Dave Martholomeo. And that's when the band recorded Fast Domino. Yeah. The band recorded Fast Domino, I think I was here. Maybe a year and a half. Back a year and a half after, you know, when we recorded Fast Domino.
Mm-hmm.
We had been scuffling, trying to make records before that to get something to go, you know.

The old J&M studio moved on Governor Nichols.
Were some of them made over on Rampart Street in those days? That's right.
I remember that. I think that's where the first record was made on Rampart Street. About stuff.
About stuff. About stuff. About stuff. About stuff. Yeah, that's what...

Yeah, that was taken...

I used to go there every week when I was in New York.

Yeah, yeah.

What does he do? Have to change the strings entirely from high to low?
No, he really plays left over right. He's the honest one I know that plays left over right.

But keeps the string up the same way. Mm-hmm. I know a bass player that does that too, a white bass player, Sherwood Manson, and Hank. He keeps his tune. He can play your bass, but he plays it left hand. Looks fun.
Yeah, thank you for showing us those photos.
Did you ever, Ernest, do you ever play any wind instruments? Have you ever tried to blow on anything at all?
Well, uh, a little of it in the service, playing marches. Oh, in the brass band? No, we played music.
Brass band?
No, military, we had military, we had concert band, and we had swing band.
What did you play?
I played the E-flat alto horn. The, uh, uh, I switched to cymbals.
Like the mellophone, you mean the regular brass horn, huh?
Yeah, it's like the mellophone. Yeah. In fact, the mellophone, this card is the alto horn for the mellophone.
I thought maybe when you said E-flat alto, it might have been the sax. The sax, C-flat alto sax.
No.
No saxophone. Ever played any reed instruments? Just the alto horn.
I started practicing tenor saxophone, but, uh, during the time I was in the service, it collected all the instruments just before I got out, you know? Uh-huh. And I stopped.
When you were a kid, did you ever follow the brass band parades around here?
Well, my parents didn't allow me to do much of that. You didn't get out much of the speech either.
I know some kids did and others didn't. I just wondered. Uh-huh.
Well, I was quite young when I was 17 years old. Yeah, that's right.
You were, from the date you gave me, I thought you must be very young.

Right. And I couldn't do much of that before. I went to a few dances. Uh, I used to admire Pichon and, uh, the Senn and Desvien. Uh, they used to let me go to dances after I got around the age of fifteen, sixteen years old. So, I had to be at home at a certain time.

Who were your favorite guitar players? Naturally, your father, who was a good guitar player, would have been one. But, uh, were there any other guitar players around here that you liked and would go to here? Or any?
tell us in the country that you, even on records, who were your favorite guitar players?
Well on records, during that time, Charlotte Christian for Swing and Les Paul for Technique. Yeah. I mean, that was my two favorite guitar players.
Did you ever hear of Charlie Christian in person or just on the record?

I didn't get a chance, I was unfortunate. Yeah, I did. And Charlie Christian died just before I went to country in the service. And, well in town, Buddy Charles, Irvin Charles is his name. I used to admire him, admire him play with Cindy Desby. And Homer Eugene. Two favorite guitar players around town.
Did you ever take any lessons from them?
Well no.
Mostly just your father and your teacher. Teacher.
As far as that instrument is concerned, I went to GI school for harmony. Oh yeah. And I took some ear training and stuff. I went to school about two years and a half.

Is that when Grunewald's head up on Camp Street or some place? I remember that. Quite a few fellows were up there, I remember. We were just about out of tape. Is there any other thing you'd like to add about your life story?
Well, I still haven't got as far as I want to go.
I guess everyone feels that in music. Keep learning.

I like to make money, it's true, but certain bands I would like to play with. I like to play some Dixon Land. I like to play some modern things. I like to get with a band that's playing more variety of things. I'm working with a band now, but that's playing a variety of music. I like to play some other things. I like to play some other things.

segments.title: Opening: name, birth date and birthplace
segments.summary: McLean gives his name and says he was born in 1925 near St. Philip Street.

segments.title: Earliest musical memory: godfather Kid Rene's band
segments.summary: He recalls his godfather's band, Kid Rene, when he was about seven.

segments.title: Learning guitar from his father and learning to read
segments.summary: The guitar was around the house; his father gave him a guitar at 11, taught him chords, and he learned to read at 14 or 15 as father worked the WPA band.

segments.title: Schooling and music in school
segments.summary: He attended grammar school with no band, and music reading was not taught to ordinary pupils.

segments.title: First bands: Kid Howard and Don Raymond
segments.summary: He worked with Kid Howard, struggled with unfamiliar tunes, then enjoyed playing with Don Raymond; Dixieland standards and waltzes.

segments.title: Leaving Don Raymond's band for World War II service
segments.summary: He left Don Raymond's band for the service about ten months after the war began.

segments.title: Looking at photographs: the WPA band and uncle Joshua Haynes
segments.summary: Photos are brought out; the WPA band is spotted, and Richard McLean identifies his uncle Joshua Haynes, photographed in Chicago with a singing club.

segments.title: Richard McLean names the musicians in the WPA band photo
segments.summary: Richard McLean and Allen identify band members in the large photo, many names garbled, including Louis Dumaine, Willie Humphrey, Joe Howard and the father himself as a boy.

segments.title: Finishing the WPA photo: trumpets and other names
segments.summary: They finish naming the trumpets and others in the picture, including George McCollum, Louis Dumaine and Gilbert Young.

segments.chapter: Guitar, recordings and Johnny St. Cyr
segments.title: Guitars, strings of lessons and picking style
segments.summary: He used Gibson guitars, no electric at first; his father taught him the MacNeil method; he always used the pick.

segments.chapter: Guitar, recordings and Johnny St. Cyr
segments.title: Recording with Johnny St. Cyr and playing solos
segments.summary: Allen mentions St. Cyr's praise; Ernest recorded with him on Southland, including The Pearls, single-string solos, and he discusses strings.

segments.chapter: Fats Domino and rock and roll years
segments.title: Current work with Dave Bartholomew's band
segments.summary: He does spot jobs with Dave Bartholomew's band, called a rock and roll band that plays variety.

segments.chapter: Fats Domino and rock and roll years
segments.title: Recording with Fats Domino
segments.summary: He worked and recorded with Fats Domino, playing on about half his records, and missed a Roy Brown session before Fats started.

segments.title: After the service: Paul Barbarin and the Famous Door group
segments.summary: Back in 1946 he played with Paul Barbarin for six months, then at the Famous Door with Edgar Blanchard, vibes and bass.

segments.title: With Dave Bartholomew, Joe Liggins and the California trip
segments.summary: He worked with Bartholomew in 1947-48, left with Joe Liggins for California, returned, and the band recorded Fats Domino at the J&M studio.

segments.title: Photo of Lloyd Price at the Apollo and the Four Gondoliers
segments.summary: Looking at a photo, they discuss playing with Lloyd Price in New York at the Apollo, and the Famous Door group.

segments.title: Left-handed guitar players
segments.summary: They discuss left-handed guitarists including Kimble and Bill Jennings; the session wraps with thanks for the photos.

segments.title: Wind instruments and military bands
segments.summary: In the service he played E-flat alto horn in concert and swing bands and began tenor saxophone.

segments.title: Brass band parades and dances as a teenager
segments.summary: His parents limited his outings; he admired Pichon and Desvigne's bands at dances from age fifteen.

segments.title: Favorite guitar players
segments.summary: He names Charlie Christian and Les Paul, and local guitarists Irvin Charles and Homer Eugene; no lessons from them.

segments.title: GI school harmony and ear training
segments.summary: In the service he attended GI school for harmony and ear training for about two and a half years.

segments.title: Closing: ambitions in music
segments.summary: He says he still has not gone as far as he wants and wants to play Dixieland and modern in a varied band.
